story_text.value:
Hey there! I'm Rafa, founder of Duckity.

Have you ever been stopped by "prove you're a human" before logging in, signing up, or sending a friend request? Your users have too, and it sucks. Duckity allows you to define what good behavior looks like instead, and deters any activity going against that with invisible CPU work and temporary freezes that slow down malicious activity.

You get - Completely invisible protection, - Silk-smooth UX, - Way more powerful customization of its behavior, - To ditch captchas!

Bots = bad, humans = good doesn't hold up anymore. People use AI agents to do things on their behalf, and they shouldn't be treated as adversarial. Meanwhile, is spam any good as long as it's human-made?

Also, Duckity is backed by a cryptography primitive called a VDF. Since crypto is cross-platform, so is Duckity! If you have a native app, it's a great moment to bring login flows in-app while staying protected. I'm using it on my package manager, which lets me sign up and log in users directly from the terminal.

I'm still working on it a lot, and I made sure to write good docs to help you get started. Any feedback, tips, or info is really useful and more than welcome.

title.value: Show HN: Duckity – Abuse protection for the AI agent era

story_text.value:
Hi HN!

I built a tool to make it easy to explore interaction nets visually in the browser.

Interaction nets are a model of computation based on local graph rewriting. They allow for deterministic, massively parallel evaluation without the variable-binding overhead of traditional lambda calculus.

I've been thinking about interaction nets for a while and realised that I just didn't have a good intuition for them. I found it hard to visualise how they worked, what sorts of programs you can express with them, what shape those programs take, and what executing programs actually feels like in practice.

This lets you explore all of these with what is hopefully an intuitive UX. Both desktop and mobile are supported.

You can explore untyped, typed, and polarised interaction nets. You can either turn types and polarity off, make them optional, or require them. Turning types/polarities on restricts which agents' ports can be wired together, and thus reduces the number of interaction rules you need to account for.

A number of examples are included so you can start exploring some interesting computations right away.

Playground: https://netties.adler.dev GitHub: https://github.com/Arrow7000/netties

I'd love feedback on usability and if there are any other features or example nets you'd like to see.

title.value: Show HN: I built an interactive visual playground for interaction nets

story_text.value:
Before Recursive Super Intelligence.. a lot of alpha can be squeezed by recursively improve humans.. Dont you think? That's the idea of Recursive Human Intelligence.

Practically: it is a desktop that reads Claude Code, Codex, Pi chats, groups them into patterns and gives you specific feedback: touching habits that cost you time.

It is bring-your-own LLM; in terms of data privacy it is operating on things you already shared with LLMs.

I have gotten some good feedback myself already: on how I wrongly prompt sometimes, so it suggested a course I can take will and a book on MLOps to fill some gaps I miss.

I hope it does the same for you! Feel free to contribute :>

story_text.value:
I assume everyone has seen the supposedly portal "paradox" where a blue portal comes smashing down on a cube and people argue if it shoots out the orange portal or not.

Well, I built a simulation with a set of scenarios to look at, each introducing a new concept, slowly building up to the conclusion. In the end, everyone should hopefully be convinced that only one solution makes sense.

I am more than happy to collect feedback and suggestions. Are the explanations clear? Is the pace good or should I spend more time on a specific concept? Do you have other scenarios in mind that are worth showing?
